title: Dynamic functional connectivity reveals evolving neural activity states of alcohol-seeking in rats
content:
by Yujing Zhang, Nicholas M. Timme, Mintao Liu, Christopher C. Lapish, Joaquín Goñi

The brain mechanisms underlying persistent alcohol-seeking in Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remain incompletely understood. To investigate this behavior, we characterized the temporal evolution of neural activity states in the anterior cingulate cortex of freely behaving rats performing an aversion-resistant drinking (ARD) task. Alcohol-preferring (P) rats were assessed, as they reliably exhibit ARD when alcohol is devalued with the bitter tastant quinine. P rats were compared with Wistar rats, which progress slower to ARD, as indicated by cessation of drinking following quinine devaluation. Using dynamic functional connectivity analyses of spike-train recordings, we identified latent neural states corresponding to seeking and non-seeking phases. We then integrated the latent-state decoding of neural activity with a seeking intensity model derived from the observed drinking behavior. This framework revealed that the decoded latent neural states closely tracked behavior. Furthermore, during alcohol-reinforced sessions, neural and behavioral measures of drinking or non-drinking states were strongly aligned in both strains. However, after alcohol devaluation, this alignment diverged in P rats but remained consistent in Wistars. The inability of P rats to acquire stable neural states following devaluation suggests impaired formation of latent states as a neural mechanism of ARD, offering insights into the cognitive vulnerabilities that may sustain AUD.
